# Getting started

## Loading packages


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(sf, ggstatplot, tmap, tidyverse, knitr,GWmodel)
```
:::


## Loading and Preparing Data

We will

- import the Hunan shapefile and parse it into a sf polygon feature object

- Import Hunan_2012.csv file and parse it into a tibble data.frame

- Join hunan and hunan_2012 data frames and tidy the data table by retaining NAME_2,ID_3, NAME_3, Country, GDPPC, GIO, Agri and Service

So step 1, import the data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Hunan county boundary layer
hunan <- st_read("data/geospatial/hunan/Hunan.shp")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


```{.r .cell-code}
#This is the csv Hunan local development indicators 
#This will be in the  R dataframe class
hunan_2012<- read_csv("data/aspatial/Hunan_2012.csv")
```
:::


Second, we will ensure that hunan is a polygon and the hunan_2012 csv is a tibble dataframe


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
class(hunan) 
```

```

```


:::




:::
:::


Finally, we will join the 2 datasets


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hunan_sf <- left_join(hunan,hunan_2012) %>%
  select(1:3, 7, 15,16,31,32)
```
:::


::: callout-note
1.  Just do the joining to the 2 datasets first (without the select line)
2.  Go to R studio environment interface (top right) and pick out the columns we want
3.  Add the select line with the columns we want.
:::

# Mapping GDPPC 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# To edit the entire plot size, can experiment around with it :D
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 6
#| echo: false
basemap <- tm_shape(hunan_sf) + 
  tm_polygons()+
  tm_text("NAME_3",size=0.5)

gdppc <- qtm(hunan_sf,"GDPPC")+
  tm_layout(
    legend.position = c("left","bottom"))
tmap_arrange(basemap,gdppc,asp=1,ncol=2)
```

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hunan_sp <- hunan_sf %>%
  as_Spatial()
```

# Geographically Weighted Summary Statistics (GSWW) with adaptive bandwidth 

## Determine adaptive Bandwidth 

### cross validation 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bw_CV <- bw.gwr(GDPPC ~ 1,# only picking one variable which is GDPpercapita
                data = hunan_sp,
                approach = "CV",
                adaptive = TRUE,
                kernel = "bisquare",
                longlat = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Adaptive bandwidth: 62 CV score: 15515442343 
Adaptive bandwidth: 46 CV score: 14937956887 
Adaptive bandwidth: 36 CV score: 14408561608 
Adaptive bandwidth: 29 CV score: 14198527496 
Adaptive bandwidth: 26 CV score: 13898800611 
Adaptive bandwidth: 22 CV score: 13662299974 
Adaptive bandwidth: 22 CV score: 13662299974 
```


:::
:::


### AICc


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bw_AIC <- bw.gwr(GDPPC ~ 1,
                  data = hunan_sp,
                  approach = "AICc",
                  adaptive = TRUE,
                  kernel = "bisquare",
                  longlat = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Adaptive bandwidth (number of nearest neighbours): 62 AICc value: 1923.156 
Adaptive bandwidth (number of nearest neighbours): 46 AICc value: 1920.469 
Adaptive bandwidth (number of nearest neighbours): 36 AICc value: 1917.324 
Adaptive bandwidth (number of nearest neighbours): 29 AICc value: 1916.661 
Adaptive bandwidth (number of nearest neighbours): 26 AICc value: 1914.897 
Adaptive bandwidth (number of nearest neighbours): 22 AICc value: 1914.045 
Adaptive bandwidth (number of nearest neighbours): 22 AICc value: 1914.045 
```


:::
:::


### Computing geographically weighted summary statistics 

The code chunk below computes geographically weighted summary statistics by using gwss() of GWmodel package. The analysis is performed using adaptive distance weighted. The distance is derived using AICc method and the kernel method is bi-square.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gwstat<-gwss(data=hunan_sp,
             vars="GDPPC",
             bw=bw_AIC,
             kernel="bisquare",
             quantile=TRUE, 
             adaptive=TRUE,
             longlat = T)
```
:::


::: callout-note
gwss support 5 kernel methods , namely Gaussian, exponential, bi-square, Tricube and boxcar. Repeat the code chunk above with different kernel methods and compare their results visually.
:::

## Preparing Output data 

::: callout-important
gwss() with quantile argument computes eight local summary statistics, namely: local means,local standard deviations, local variance, local skew, local coefficients of variation, local medians, local interquartile ranges, and local quantile imbalances. they are output in SDF data frame.
:::

Code chunk below is used to extract SDF data table from gwss object output from gwss() for subsequent geovilisation. It will be converted into data.frame by using as.data.frame().


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gwstat_df <- as.data.frame(gwstat$SDF)
```
:::


Next the cbind() is used to append the newly derived data.frame onto *hunan_sf* sf data.frame


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hunan_gstat <-cbind(hunan_sf,gwstat_df)
```
:::
